newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank merger talk revives as insurers marry.
newsitem.headline: German bank merger talk revives as insurers marry.

text.p: Investors' expectations that the German financial services sector faces a shake-up have grown following recent news of a merger of two insurers under Munich Re, analysts said on Wednesday.

Banking stocks have come back in favour in the two weeks since Munich Re said it would merge its two affiliates Victoria Holding AG and Hamburg-Mannheimer AG to form Germany's second largest primary insurer after Allianz AG.

"When things start to happen in the insurance sector the speculation spills over into bank stocks," said Stefan Ermisch, banking analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank. "The banking sector will consolidate in some form, especially in domestic retail banking."
Top bankers have consistently dismissed the prospect of an early outbreak of mergers among private sector banks and say the public banks will be the first to consolidate.

Events over the the last year have confirmed that view, with mergers mainly confined to state-owned regional banks, most notably Norddeutsche Landesbank and Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG, which in May announced plans to merge.
But privately, bankers admit that consolidation among the major listed commercial banks is inevitable and will come in a chain reaction once the first big player makes a move.
"It only takes someone to pull their finger out of the dyke to start the flood," one senior banker at an international bank said this week.
One Munich-based banker said last week that big changes may come as early as this year.
"I don't agree when people say this will be a very slow development," he said. "Things could move fast because it really only takes one decision. We could see big changes in the next six months."
The views of Munich bankers and insurers are particularly relevant because they will be at the heart of any reshaping of Germany's banking market.

The rationale behind mergers is clear. Germany is regarded as heavily overbanked with more than 3,600 commercial, public and cooperative banks battling for market share, and a rate of one branch per 1,100 inhabitants.
The top five banks, led by Deutsche Bank AG, have a joint market share of just 14 percent and are struggling to make their costly retail branch networks more efficient.
Three possible scenarios for a revamp in the private sector have emerged.

Firstly, the two Munich-based banks Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechselbank AG (Hypo-Bank), the number four and five respectively among the listed commercial banks, may join forces.
That would be the "Bavarian solution" sought by local politicians but some analysts see little benefit in a merger of two banks that are relatively weak in investment banking.
Also, the two would encounter stiff political opposition to the branch closures and job cuts that would make the link-up profitable.
The second option is that Dresdner Bank AG, the number two bank, may merge with Hypo-Bank.

Analysts say insurance giant Allianz AG, which owns stakes of roughly 22 percent in the two banks, may put pressure on them to join forces although some say the insurer may not have sufficient clout to push this through.
Thirdly, Dresdner and Allianz may intensify cooperation, possibly deciding to expand their asset management businesses together, analysts said.
Allianz chief executive Henning Schulte-Noelle last week kept the rumour mill grinding when he was quoted as saying he would not bet on whether there would be changes in the short-term.
That marked a change of tune from the end of May, when he said changes would take place only in the medium or long term.
Market talk of mergers took off on July 10 1996, when Deutsche disclosed it had amassed a 5.21 percent stake in Vereinsbank AG, shares of which have soared more than 80 percent since.
Deutsche has said the move was aimed at deterring potential bidders for Vereinsbank and that it had no immediate plans to increase the stake.
